title: Dover — the train ran out to the ship
subtopic: 2 — Dover, and the hour and a quarter of open sea
learning_goal: Know that the boat train ran out along the Admiralty Pier so you stepped from carriage to deck, that the cliffs are chalk and France is 32 km off, and that the crossing was a byword for misery; feel cold air and open water.

narration.script:
Dover, and a night boat. Charles Dickens crossed here in 1863 and wrote it down. On the deck, he watches the train come to him: 'A screech, a bell, and two red eyes come gliding down the Admiralty Pier.'

The railway ran out along the pier, over the water, to the steamer. By Fogg's night the rails ran out along it, so his boat train would have set him down beside the ship — carriage to deck, without touching a street.

Above the harbour, the cliffs. Chalk, about a hundred metres high, and about a hundred million years old. France is thirty-two kilometres away, and on a clear day you can see it. The French call this water la Manche — the sleeve. Verne never mentions any of it.

An hour and a quarter of open water. Dickens again, on his fellow passengers: they 'lie about in melancholy bundles, as if they were sorted out for the laundress.' One man holds an umbrella up the whole way over.

Our pictures are daylight, and a lifetime late. Fogg crossed in the middle of the night.

production_notes: SEGMENT 2 (130 s, fill 60 %, ceiling 185 words). Three beats: pier 0-45, cliffs 45-70, sea 70-130. THE SECOND LOAD-BEARING SILENCE: 70-82 s, the sea holds with the wave bed and nothing else. There is a second, smaller authored silence at 62-70 s, after the cliffs. DO NOT staged this at Dover Priory station (the fact sheet's own instruction) — the beat is the pier. TWO MEDIA ENTRIES PER SHOT, the A8 pattern: the sea window 70-105 s is M-201 in the film and M-222 in the player; 105-130 s is M-202 (Méliès) in the film and M-225 in the player.
